content.title: About
content.content: Light butter is a reduced‑fat butter (usually 10‑15 % fat). It is made from cream where a portion of the butterfat is removed, then the remaining fat is blended with water and sometimes a small amount of vegetable oil to improve texture. Light butter retains a buttery taste while providing fewer calories and less saturated fat than regular butter.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Light butter is popular in dietetic cooking where lower calorie content is desired.
Its fat content is typically 10‑15 %, compared with about 80 % in regular butter.
Emulsifiers and stabilizers are often added to maintain a smooth, spreadable texture.
It can be produced from cow’s or goat’s cream.
In some markets it is sold under names like “light butter” or “low‑calorie butter.”

items.title: Reduced saturated fat intake
items.content: The lower fat content helps decrease overall saturated fat consumption, which may positively affect cholesterol levels.

items.title: Source of vitamins A and D
items.content: Like regular butter, light butter provides fat‑soluble vitamins A and D important for vision, immunity, and bone health.

items.title: Lower calorie density
items.content: Light butter provides roughly 150‑180 kcal per 100 g, considerably less than traditional butter (~720 kcal).

items.title: Contains conjugated linoleic acid (CLA)
items.content: A small amount of CLA remains in light butter and may have beneficial metabolic effects.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Light butter contains milk proteins that can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Additive content
items.content: Emulsifiers, stabilizers, and small amounts of vegetable oils may be present, which some diets avoid.

items.title: May not fully replace regular butter in baking
items.content: Reduced fat can affect dough structure, so recipe adjustments may be needed.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use light butter for spreading on bread, making sauces, sautéing over medium heat, and baking when you want to cut calories. It can be combined with regular butter to achieve desired texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store light butter in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C in its original packaging or an airtight container. For long‑term storage it can be frozen at –18 °C, though texture may change after thawing.
